topic:everyone-is-a-developer.title: Everyone who can brief an agent is a developer now
topic:everyone-is-a-developer.why: The opening frame of the edition: the reader is already a developer if they can describe what they want to an agent; Gen Z in 2026, the citizen developer, your own language as a programming language, and optimism against the burnout mood.

topic:explorers-villagers-town-planners.title: Explorers, villagers and town planners (Wardley's frame)
topic:explorers-villagers-town-planners.why: The structure of the whole book: where the reader sits, what explorer coding is good for, and the handover to people who maintain and answer for software; the 2018 pioneers/settlers/town planners outline grown up.

topic:getting-the-job.title: Getting the job: hired for the workflow, act as the job you want
topic:getting-the-job.why: The practical promise of the book: why October 2026 is a moment of opportunity, what employers want (AI operators), how to stand out when candidates look equal, and how to work in public so others can help you.

topic:publish-in-public.title: Publish, publish, publish: your own newsroom
topic:publish-in-public.why: Linkable work is the CV now: a site published by an agent from voice memos, an article behind every answer, small finished pieces over big batches.

topic:working-with-agents.title: How to work with agents: briefs, voice, one shared state
topic:working-with-agents.why: The day-to-day craft: brief by voice, review on the phone, focused sessions with roles, lessons and debriefs as memory, a daily brief, and reading sources in full.

topic:facts-and-the-record.title: Facts, evidence and the record
topic:facts-and-the-record.why: Make fact-based decisions (on the 2018 cover) in the agent era: think out loud and let the record check you, count rather than remember, review as a record, and distrust self-reports.

topic:human-in-the-loop.title: Where a person belongs: one-way doors, two-way doors and blast radius
topic:human-in-the-loop.why: The judgement a newcomer needs before letting an agent act: how cheap is it to undo, how large is the blast radius, and how the record moves the line over time.

topic:controlling-your-agent.title: Controlling your agent: mandate, reach and hope versus enforcement
topic:controlling-your-agent.why: Before you give an agent access, write down what it is for and what it can reach; rules in a prompt are hope, rules in a hook or platform are enforcement; behaviour, decision and workflow are different questions.

topic:security-agent-era.title: Security for the agent era: least code, supply chain, secrets, learning to hack
topic:security-agent-era.why: Code is a liability; the next maintainer is an agent; check skills and dependencies before installing; keep secrets out of the chat; learning to hack is still how you learn how things work.

topic:open-source.title: Open source: contribute, fork, and why it protects everyone
topic:open-source.why: Open source remains the newcomer's best door (first PR, public work) and is becoming the most secure software; the fork protects founders, customers and investors; constraints make better products.

topic:building-blocks.title: Building blocks: cloud, serverless, free models, git and CI
topic:building-blocks.why: What a non-specialist can assemble today, mostly free, with an agent doing the one-time setup; git as a standard; CI; knowing what tokens cost.

topic:graphs-memory.title: Graphs, memory and your future self
topic:graphs-memory.why: Graphs as the way of thinking (not just Dot): brief from a graph, maintain it rather than perfect it, search as navigation; and keep your work linkable and backed up so your future self can find it.

topic:be-a-founder.title: Be a founder (or a one-person service)
topic:be-a-founder.why: Agents make execution cheap, so the expert can build first; what investors select for; technology that works before the use case; small agent-run services and pay-after-value models.

topic:civic-and-history.title: Civic responsibility: hacking a country, sovereignty, your language
topic:civic-and-history.why: Dinis's Portugal talks as the then-now of civic responsibility: to hack means to solve problems; what regulation delivered; small countries can lead in code now that everyone can build.

topic:making-of.title: How this book was made (the last part)
topic:making-of.why: The edition's own workflow as the final worked example: repository and vault, agents in roles, voice memos, the record, review on the record, three voices, co-written with Claude and the memo-to-word ratio.

topic:direction-is-the-scarce-skill.title: Direction is the scarce skill: the place of highest leverage, knowing when to stop, starting without knowing the end
topic:direction-is-the-scarce-skill.why: When anyone can brief an agent, building stops being the bottleneck and choosing what to build, and when to stop, becomes the skill employers and users pay for. This is the junior's version of seniority, and it answers the 2018 life-patterns outlines (habits, the zone, start with why) that had no article.

topic:your-first-workspace.title: Your first workspace: from one Claude Project to a team of agents, safely
topic:your-first-workspace.why: The first pass flagged this as gap 1, with no how-to in scope. Four imported articles together make a step-by-step path: a folder per person in Drive with a Claude Project, then habits, then the agent's own mailbox and seat, with agents kept off your laptop. It could also sit as the opening chapter of working-with-agents.

topic:shipped-means-the-user-has-it.title: Shipped means the user has it: tests, CI and going slow to go fast
topic:shipped-means-the-user-has-it.why: Fills the testing/TDD gap with stories rather than theory. A green build is not a release, tests that never run are not tests, the handover from explorer to villager is a refactor you can prove, and synthetic users check what the user sees. Answers 2018 TDD, CI-Testing, SRE and devops.

concept:explorer-villager-town-planner.title: explorer / villager / town planner
concept:explorer-villager-town-planner.definition: Simon Wardley's three kinds of people and work: explorers build the new by trying, villagers harden and maintain what people start to depend on, town planners industrialise it and answer for it in production.

concept:explorer-coding.title: explorer coding
concept:explorer-coding.definition: The newsroom's name for vibe coding: anyone with a need explores it by building, with the fast feedback loop that made spreadsheets win; not ready to be 'in line' until villagers and town planners take it on.

concept:the-handover-deployment-gap.title: the handover (deployment gap)
concept:the-handover-deployment-gap.definition: The step from a prototype to a tool people rely on is not a place to stop but a handover from explorers to villagers and town planners, who add the non-functional requirements.

concept:citizen-developer.title: citizen developer
concept:citizen-developer.definition: The employee, owner or expert who now builds full applications: the spreadsheet grown up, good news rather than a risk.

concept:the-prototype-is-the-best-brief.title: the prototype is the best brief
concept:the-prototype-is-the-best-brief.definition: What someone builds for themselves says what they actually want, in a form that runs, better than any requirements document.

concept:ai-operator.title: AI operator
concept:ai-operator.definition: Dinis's term for the people companies need now: not model builders but people who use the tools and workflows to get things done.

concept:hired-for-the-workflow.title: hired for the workflow
concept:hired-for-the-workflow.definition: Being hired for the ability to run agentic workflows, as people were once hired for breaking apps or building websites, degree or no degree; the edge shows when candidates look equal, starting with the application.

concept:act-as-the-job-you-want.title: act as the job you want
concept:act-as-the-job-you-want.definition: If you are looking for a job you have time: do the job before you have it, in public, so it can be linked: reach does not matter, the link lets the people who want to help you forward it.

concept:your-own-newsroom.title: your own newsroom
concept:your-own-newsroom.definition: A personal publishing loop: voice memo in, an agent researches, checks and writes in your voice, a validated static site out, readers pay a little if it is useful.

concept:omnichannel-programming.title: omnichannel programming
concept:omnichannel-programming.definition: Programming across voice, chat, phone, IDE and pull requests where every channel reads and writes one shared state (git, vaults, briefs, graphs), as against multichannel, where each keeps its own copy.

concept:brief.title: brief
concept:brief.definition: A written request an agent session can start from: what is asked, what exists, what remains; the unit of work between a person and agents.

concept:one-way-door-two-way-door.title: one-way door / two-way door
concept:one-way-door-two-way-door.definition: Amazon's test, used here for agents: a two-way door can be undone cheaply (a page correction), a one-way door cannot (a sent email); the cost of undoing decides where a person belongs.

concept:blast-radius.title: blast radius
concept:blast-radius.definition: What an output or a row of an agent's reach would cost if it went wrong in full today; put the person where it is large and the output cannot be undone (defined fully in footprint-and-blast-radius, outside the surveyed set).

concept:agent-behaviour-policy-abp.title: Agent Behaviour Policy (ABP)
concept:agent-behaviour-policy-abp.definition: For one agent in one deployment: what it can reach, what it was authorised to do, the gap between the two, and what actually stands in the way of each capability.

concept:mandate-reach-and-the-gap.title: mandate, reach and the gap
concept:mandate-reach-and-the-gap.definition: Mandate is what the agent (or credential) is for; reach is everything it can touch; the gap between them is the risk, and every supply-chain attack used it.

concept:hope-based-security.title: hope-based security
concept:hope-based-security.definition: Rules written in a prompt and kept only if the model keeps them: better than nothing, not enough on its own.

concept:hooks.title: hooks
concept:hooks.definition: Small programs the agent's harness runs at fixed points (before and after a tool call, on prompt, on stop) that can see, block or rewrite actions; guardrails, not walls.

concept:behaviour-decision-and-workflow-.title: behaviour, decision and workflow policies
concept:behaviour-decision-and-workflow-.definition: Behaviour says what an agent may do, decision says who chooses at a branch point and on what evidence, workflow says in what order.

concept:allowed-is-not-right.title: allowed is not right
concept:allowed-is-not-right.definition: Every control can pass and the outcome still be wrong (a $150 refund where $120 was owed); proving the right outcome needs a written definition of right.

concept:lethal-trifecta.title: lethal trifecta
concept:lethal-trifecta.definition: Simon Willison's term the newsroom uses: private data, untrusted content and a way out in one agent or skill; any agent with all three needs a control even if honest.

concept:the-record.title: the record
concept:the-record.definition: What was actually done, kept outside anyone's memory (commits, briefs, transcripts, versions); 'the record catches up with the instinct', so thinking out loud becomes safe, and peer review moves to before publishing (confirmed, corrected or not found).

concept:review-on-the-record.title: review on the record
concept:review-on-the-record.definition: Every review is a file written once against published criteria, and every finding is answered: fixed in which version, declined and why, or open.

concept:self-report.title: self-report
concept:self-report.definition: An agent's own logs and account of itself; evidence written outside the agent is more honest and still needs reading.

concept:code-is-a-liability-minimal-viab.title: code is a liability / minimal viable code path
concept:code-is-a-liability-minimal-viab.definition: Every shipped line is a capability someone may misuse; the future is the smallest code that does exactly the job, made safe by model-built tests and maps.

concept:ephemeral-town-planner-services.title: ephemeral town planner services
concept:ephemeral-town-planner-services.definition: A better name for serverless: scales to zero, costs nothing idle, starts fast, a commodity exposed for others; test: if it bills you by the hour when idle, it is not serverless.

concept:fractal-semantic-graph.title: fractal semantic graph
concept:fractal-semantic-graph.definition: Knowledge held as a graph with an ontology and taxonomy per element, each part in its own vocabulary, every node openable as a graph of its own; briefs come from the slice you need.

concept:the-fork-next-door.title: the fork next door
concept:the-fork-next-door.definition: In open source anyone can fork, which protects founders, customers and investors from each other; forks take hold only when someone stops executing.

concept:every-part-buys-the-next.title: every part buys the next
concept:every-part-buys-the-next.definition: The subject buys the first line, the first line buys the paragraph, the paragraph buys the email: open with the short answer in plain text.

concept:three-voices.title: three voices
concept:three-voices.definition: Me alone, me through an agent, an agent in its own voice; every byline should say which.

concept:your-own-key.title: your own key
concept:your-own-key.definition: Using a model provider with your own API key called straight from the browser, so nobody else holds the key or pays for your questions.

concept:wardley-map.title: Wardley map
concept:wardley-map.definition: A graph with context in two directions: a value chain anchored on a user and a need, and an evolution axis (usually genesis, custom built, product, commodity, though the axis is a choice). Read out like a story, it says what to build, what to buy, and where a market exists. Every node is itself a map.

concept:place-of-highest-leverage.title: place of highest leverage
concept:place-of-highest-leverage.definition: Where the most value can be added now, nothing blocks you, and you can start without knowing how the whole problem ends. It is not where the biggest problem is. Each step is shipped and used before the next is chosen.

concept:direction-is-the-scarce-thing.title: direction is the scarce thing
concept:direction-is-the-scarce-thing.definition: Agents can build in any direction; what they cannot generate is the sense of what to build next and when to stop. People with a direction are the input to the loop, not displaced by it.

concept:knowing-when-to-stop.title: knowing when to stop
concept:knowing-when-to-stop.definition: The judgement that experience gives people (who the attackers are, the phase of the business, the bottleneck, what good enough looks like). Agents lack it by design, so it has to be supplied as constraints: a mandate, a stop named in advance, a narrow scope.

concept:footprint.title: footprint
concept:footprint.definition: What the agent actually did, read afterwards from the record and compared with its mandate. It is the partner of blast radius, which is what a reach would cost if used in full.

concept:green-does-not-mean-live.title: green does not mean live
concept:green-does-not-mean-live.definition: Shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository: a release has to check the boundary the user is on, not only the ones CI can see.

concept:an-agent-is-a-session-with-a-foc.title: an agent is a session with a focus
concept:an-agent-is-a-session-with-a-foc.definition: An agent is a named session (an @name) that reads a few documents about the project and a role.md saying what it does and does not do. One session per topic, never mixed threads.

concept:drafts-never-send.title: drafts, never send
concept:drafts-never-send.definition: The rule for an agentic inbox: agents read, label and draft, and a person reads, edits and presses send. The agent has its own mailbox and its own Claude seat, never yours.

concept:threat-ladder-draw-the-line-wher.title: threat ladder (draw the line where the attacker is)
concept:threat-ladder-draw-the-line-wher.definition: Security starts from who the threat agent is, the attack vector and how sophisticated it is. On a ladder from your own mistakes up to states, plan to the rung that matches what you protect, do the basics consistently, and write down what you accept above that rung.

concept:every-risk-is-already-accepted.title: every risk is already accepted
concept:every-risk-is-already-accepted.definition: Every risk an organisation has is already accepted by somebody, so the questions are who accepted it and until when.

concept:agents-decide-people-answer.title: agents decide, people answer
concept:agents-decide-people-answer.definition: Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, because the grant is the moment of authorisation.

concept:agency-scale.title: agency scale
concept:agency-scale.definition: Seven levels from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source. A decision is capped by its weakest ingredient (options, context, time, incentives, escalation, authority). Below level 3 the person deciding carries liability without agency.

concept:every-mistake-added-a-rule.title: every mistake added a rule
concept:every-mistake-added-a-rule.definition: The complexity trap for agent operators: each mistake becomes a rule, the prompt grows, compaction comes sooner and new mistakes follow. The way out is small, tested, shipped components that move right on the map and no longer need the rule.

concept:re-anchoring.title: re-anchoring
concept:re-anchoring.definition: Keeping an agent's rules in a file that a hook prints back after every summary, so the rules are restored rather than remembered, with a canary that shows they are still being read.

concept:synthetic-users.title: synthetic users
concept:synthetic-users.definition: Invented people, each with a situation, a question, what they know and what makes them leave, played by a model that drives a real browser one screenshot at a time, so it can get lost as a person would.

concept:go-slow-to-go-fast.title: go slow to go fast
concept:go-slow-to-go-fast.definition: The explorer-to-villager move done as a pure refactor, proved by the live site serving the same bytes, before adding tests and hardening.

concept:no-server-by-design.title: no server by design
concept:no-server-by-design.definition: Retire the database (files), then the back end: encrypted vaults keep the server blind, the app runs in the browser, only commodity products are left on the server, and the gaps you accept are written down.

concept:do-they-miss-it.title: do they miss it
concept:do-they-miss-it.definition: The startup test: if users would miss the product when it is gone, it is working. The people who set the roadmap have to use the product themselves.

concept:open-source-means-nobody-can-loc.title: open source means nobody can lock you in
concept:open-source-means-nobody-can-loc.definition: Open source is a copyright licence granting copying, use and change. Its real power is that nobody can lock you in. Security depends on whether somebody had the time and money to review the code.

concept:inertia-decides.title: inertia decides
concept:inertia-decides.definition: AI is available to incumbents and newcomers alike, so the outcome is decided by where each sits on the evolution axis and how much past success it has to protect.

idea:knowing-when-to-stop.title: Knowing when to stop is most of seniority
idea:knowing-when-to-stop.statement: Who the attackers are, the phase of the business, the bottleneck, what good enough looks like: experience gives people this, agents lack it, and the book has to teach the junior's version.

idea:one-way-two-way-doors.title: One-way and two-way doors, blast radius, and where a person belongs
idea:one-way-two-way-doors.statement: How cheap is it to undo decides where the human goes: put the person where the output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large; give them the why; let the record move the line over time. People approve 93% of permission prompts.

idea:agents-decide-people-answer.title: Agents decide, people answer
idea:agents-decide-people-answer.statement: Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate; also ELIZA and anthropomorphism.

idea:the-record-checks-you.title: Make fact-based decisions: think out loud and let the record check you
idea:the-record-checks-you.statement: Count rather than remember; publish only what the record supports (5 claims confirmed, 5 corrected, 2 not found); review as a record with every finding answered; distrust self-reports.

idea:mandate-reach-gap.title: Mandate, reach and the gap: hope versus enforcement
idea:mandate-reach-gap.statement: Before you give an agent access, write down what it is for and what it can reach; the gap is the risk; rules in a prompt are hope, rules in a hook or platform are enforcement; behaviour, decision and workflow policies are different things.

idea:code-is-a-liability.title: Code is a liability; the future is the smallest code that does the job
idea:code-is-a-liability.statement: Every shipped line is a capability someone may misuse (Log4j; 428 of 1,500 files ran); the next maintainer is an agent; the minimal viable code path.

idea:learn-to-hack.title: Learning to hack is still how you learn how things work: draw the line where the attacker is
idea:learn-to-hack.statement: Name the threat agent, the vector and how sophisticated it is; a ladder from your own mistakes up to states; the bookmarklet trick; to hack means to solve problems.

idea:secrets-never-in-the-chat.title: The secret goes from the drop into the tool, never into the chat
idea:secrets-never-in-the-chat.statement: Classify the credential before it touches anything; an agent told something cannot untell it; the lethal trifecta.

idea:the-fork-next-door.title: Open source means nobody can lock you in: the fork next door
idea:the-fork-next-door.statement: Anyone can fork, which protects founders, customers and investors from each other; forks take hold only when someone stops executing; six misconceptions; open source is about to become the most secure software.

idea:first-pr.title: Your first pull request: open source is still the newcomer's best door
idea:first-pr.statement: A one-file, 83-line documentation PR merged into a 9,625-commit project; contribute to the projects of the companies you want to work for.

idea:lego-blocks.title: Building blocks: cloud as Lego, free models with your own key, git as a standard
idea:lego-blocks.statement: What a non-specialist can assemble today, mostly free, with an agent doing the one-time setup; serverless as ephemeral town planner services; knowing what tokens cost.
idea:lego-blocks.notes: Costs for a newcomer is still a gap.
